core: The four outer giant planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) as a group: large size, deep atmospheres, no solid surface
Gas giants (Jupiter, Saturn) versus ice giants (Uranus, Neptune): hydrogen/helium composition versus water-ammonia-methane ices
Signature features: Jupiter's Great Red Spot and Galilean moons (named), Saturn's rings, Uranus's axial tilt, Neptune's winds
Planetary rings: why giant planets have them (general), Saturn's as the showpiece
Brief mention of giant-planet moons and magnetospheres (moons owned by sibling topic)
supporting: Relative sizes and masses of the four giant planets
Density evidence for the gas/ice distinction
Discovery history of Uranus (1781, Herschel) and Neptune (1846, mathematics)
No-hard-surface language and its careful phrasing
Ring discovery facts (Jupiter 1979 Voyager 1; Uranus 1977; Neptune 1989 Voyager 2)
outOfScope: Moons in detail (sibling topic; named and referenced only)
Solar system as a whole (sibling topic)

claims.claim: The four giant planets — Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune — are the largest planets in the solar system and are located in the outer solar system.
The giant planets do not have hard surfaces; they are mostly swirling gases and liquids above a core, so there is nowhere to land and descending probes would be crushed, melted, or vaporized.

Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants made mostly of hydrogen and helium; Jupiter has the same ingredients as a star but never grew massive enough to ignite, and Saturn is the only planet with an average density less than water.

Uranus and Neptune are ice giants: 80 percent or more of each planet's mass is a hot dense fluid of water, methane, and ammonia ices above a small rocky core, and both are denser than Saturn, indicating a composition fundamentally different from the gas giants.

Jupiter's signature features include the Great Red Spot (a giant storm bigger than Earth, observed for more than 300 years), the Galilean moons Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto (first observed by Galileo Galilei in 1610), a faint ring system discovered by Voyager 1 in 1979, and a magnetosphere so vast its tail reaches as far as Saturn's orbit.

Saturn has the most spectacular ring system of the four giant planets; its rings are made of billions of chunks of ice and rock, from dust-sized grains to house-sized blocks, thought to be pieces of comets, asteroids, or shattered moons torn apart by the planet's gravity.

Uranus rotates at a nearly 90-degree angle from the plane of its orbit, so it appears to spin on its side; it is about four times wider than Earth and gets its blue-green color from methane in its atmosphere.

Neptune is the windiest world in the solar system, with winds of more than 1,200 miles per hour (2,000 kilometers per hour) — about three times stronger than Jupiter's and nine times stronger than Earth's — despite being more than 30 times farther from the Sun than Earth; it was the first planet discovered through mathematics, in 1846.
All four giant planets have ring systems — Saturn's is the brightest and most complex — and rings are bands of countless small particles of ice and rock, not solid disks.

Each giant planet has a magnetosphere, the region its magnetic field dominates; Jupiter's is the most powerful, ballooning millions of kilometers toward the Sun and trailing a tail that extends as far as Saturn's orbit.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Uranus moon counts differ across NASA's own pages (the overview caption mentions 27 moons, the facts page says 28).
positions: NASA Uranus overview page (Webb image caption): '14 of the planet's 27 moons'
NASA Uranus facts page: 'surrounded by 13 faint rings and 28 small moons'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson avoids all moon counts; moons are a sibling topic, and the discrepancy is a NASA page inconsistency, not a lesson claim.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Terminology: some sources call all four giant planets 'gas giants' or group them as 'Jovian planets,' while NASA now reserves 'gas giants' for Jupiter and Saturn and calls Uranus and Neptune 'ice giants.'
positions: NASA Solar System overview: 'Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants. Uranus and Neptune are ice giants.'
Older popular usage applies 'gas giant' to all four; OpenStax uses 'giant planets'/'jovian planets' as the umbrella and 'ice giants' for Uranus and Neptune.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows NASA's current classification (gas giants vs ice giants) and notes 'Jovian planets' as an alternative umbrella term for the group.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Uranus axial tilt is stated as 'nearly 90 degrees' by NASA and as 98 degrees by OpenStax.
positions: NASA Uranus facts: 'rotates at a nearly 90-degree angle from the plane of its orbit'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses NASA's phrasing ('nearly 90-degree angle ... appears to spin on its side'), which is not contradicted by OpenStax's more precise 98 degrees.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's framing that 'Gas Giants is a foundational concept' with generic definitions of 'context' and 'evidence' was machine boilerplate with no factual content and was discarded.
The draft's three boilerplate questions ('Which approach best shows understanding of Gas Giants?') tested nothing factual and were replaced.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced all boilerplate draft wording with evidence-based content sourced to NASA and OpenStax.
Used NASA's careful no-hard-surface language ('don't have hard surfaces' / 'doesn't have a true surface') instead of the imprecise 'balls of gas' phrasing.
Kept moon counts out of the lesson because NASA's pages disagree (27 vs 28 for Uranus) and moons are a sibling topic; Galilean moons are named only as Jupiter's signature feature.
Used the gas-giant versus ice-giant distinction exactly as NASA states it, including the 80%-or-more water/methane/ammonia-ices composition for Uranus and Neptune.

Verified every quantitative claim (1,000 Earths inside Jupiter; Uranus about four times wider than Earth; Neptune more than 30 times farther than Earth; winds above 1,200 mph/2,000 km/h; 9.9-hour Jupiter day; Saturn less dense than water) arithmetically with python3.
rightsIssues: NASA pages are U.S. government works (public domain facts), used reference-only with fully original prose.

OpenStax Astronomy 2e is CC BY 4.0 but its pages state the book may not be ingested into large language models without permission; therefore aiIngestionAllowed is false and OpenStax content was used for fact-checking only, with no wording, figures, or tables reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: About the Planets (Solar System Overview)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports the group description of the giant planets: 'The giant planets in the outer solar system don't have hard surfaces. Instead, they have swirling gases above a core. Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants. Uranus and Neptune are ice giants.' Also supports Jupiter as the largest planet, Saturn as second largest, Uranus as third largest. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Jupiter Facts
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports: Jupiter largest and oldest planet, about 1,000 Earths could fit inside, more than twice the combined mass of the other planets; day of 9.9 hours and year of about 12 Earth years; composition similar to the Sun (mostly hydrogen and helium); 'doesn't have a true surface... mostly swirling gases and liquids'; Great Red Spot a giant storm bigger than Earth raging for hundreds of years, observed for more than 300 years, persisting because no solid surface slows it; Galilean moons Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto first observed by Galileo Galilei in 1610; faint ring system discovered by Voyager 1 in 1979, possibly dust from meteoroid impacts on inner moons; magnetosphere extending as far as Saturn's orbit; ammonia and water clouds in a hydrogen-helium atmosphere; belts and zones. Facts synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: Saturn Facts
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports: Saturn sixth planet and second largest; 'Like fellow gas giant Jupiter, Saturn is a massive ball made mostly of hydrogen and helium'; not the only planet with rings but none as spectacular or complex; only planet with average density less than water; 'doesn't have a true surface. The planet is mostly swirling gases and liquids deeper down'; rings thought to be pieces of comets, asteroids, or shattered moons torn apart by gravity, made of billions of small chunks of ice and rock from dust-sized grains to house-sized (some mountain-sized) blocks; ring system extends up to 175,000 miles (282,000 km); equatorial winds of 1,600 feet per second (500 meters per second). Facts synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: Uranus Facts
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports: Uranus seventh planet, third largest, about four times wider than Earth; 'one of two ice giants in the outer solar system (the other is Neptune)'; most (80% or more) of the mass is a hot dense fluid of icy materials (water, methane, ammonia) above a small rocky core; rotates at a nearly 90-degree angle from the plane of its orbit, appearing to spin sideways and orbit like a rolling ball; 13 faint rings; blue-green color from methane; second least dense planet (after Saturn); discovered in 1781 by William Herschel, first planet found with a telescope; Voyager 2 flyby in 1986. Facts synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: Neptune Facts
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports: Neptune eighth and most distant planet, fourth largest, more than 30 times as far from the Sun as Earth, not visible to the naked eye; first planet located through mathematical predictions (discovered 1846; first 165-year orbit completed in 2011); 'one of two ice giants in the outer solar system (the other is Uranus)'; most (80% or more) of the mass is a hot dense fluid of icy materials (water, methane, ammonia) above a small rocky core; densest of the giant planets; 'does not have a solid surface'; solar system's windiest world with winds of more than 1,200 miles per hour (2,000 km/h), about three times stronger than Jupiter's and nine times stronger than Earth's; at least five main rings and four prominent ring arcs; Voyager 2 flyby in 1989. Facts synthesized.
